class_id: a capped worker's ORDER BY points away from the backlog it was built to drain, and every row it does process is individually valid
feature: any batch worker that selects a capped slice of a queue each run — drainers, backfills, re-processors, catch-up jobs, retry sweeps — where the selection has a WHERE clause everyone reviews and an ORDER BY nobody does
symptom: the worker is built because a specific backlog exists. Its WHERE clause correctly describes the eligible POPULATION, and its cap correctly limits blast radius per run. The ORDER BY is then chosen on a plausible-sounding general principle — newest first, oldest first, alphabetical, by id — rather than by which rows carry the work. Because the backlog is almost always the tail of whatever the natural order is (that is WHY it is a backlog: the normal path already handled the head), the worker spends its first many runs on rows needing nothing. Two things then hide it. First, every row it processes is individually valid, so no row-level check, no data audit and no invariant fires — the output is correct, it is just about the wrong rows. Second, workers of this shape usually write a per-attempt ledger and exclude completed rows, so the wasted runs CONSUME the caps and mark rows done, and the log reads `attempted=N done=N` every run: a green signal over an empty set. Whoever reads week one concludes it is working. The generic test is to run the real selection query against real data BEFORE first execution and count how many of the rows it returns actually carry the work the job exists for. If the answer is zero, the ORDER BY is the defect.
first_seen: 2026-09-21 — IPODhan item 17, the closed-IPO job, caught the same night it merged (#868) by running its real selection SQL read-only against staging before the job had ever executed. `CLOSED_IPO_CANDIDATES_SQL` ordered `close_date DESC` with a cap of 10. Measured: eligible population 343; the 74 IPOs holding a stuck PENDING PROSPECTUS — the entire reason the job exists (#717) — sit at ranks 156-294, mean 231, because they are OLD, which is precisely why nothing had re-visited them. Night 1 would have reached 0 of them; nights 1-10, still 0; the first on night 16 and the last on night 30. Meanwhile the job writes a `closed_ipo_resourcing` row per attempt and excludes DONE ones, so fifteen nights of slots would have gone to IPOs needing nothing, each marked DONE, logging `attempted=10 done=10` nightly. The unit tests passed throughout: they pinned the four WHERE rules and the cap, and never the ORDER BY. Fixed in #874 by ordering on the count of PENDING documents whose type an extractor can actually read, with close_date surviving as the tie-break — proven on the same real data: 10 of the 10 rows night 1 now selects carry a stuck document, versus 0 of 10 before.
fix_prs: #874. Three parts worth copying. (1) Order by NEED — a subquery counting the rows that represent the work — with the old ordering demoted to a tie-break rather than deleted, so the original intent survives where it does no harm. (2) Restrict that count to work the job can actually DO: counting all pending documents would have ranked an IPO by rows whose types have no extractor at all (#869), which no number of visits can resolve. (3) Assert the ORDER BY as an ORDERED PAIR in the test (a regex that requires the need clause, then DESC and a comma, then the tie-break, in that order), because asserting that both clauses are merely PRESENT says nothing about which one decides — that weaker assertion would have passed against the defect.
detection_check: none built. Two candidates, both cheap. The pre-merge one is the stronger: for any capped selection query, run it against real data and assert that a non-trivial share of the returned rows carry the work the job exists for — an ordering test that can only pass for the right reason. The runtime one, for jobs already live: alert when a drainer's completion counter rises while the BACKLOG counter it is supposed to reduce does not move, over some number of consecutive runs. That is the signal that distinguishes 'working' from 'working on the wrong rows', and nothing in this repository currently computes it. Note the enabling condition here: the backlog was independently countable (`documents` with `extraction_status = 'PENDING'`), so 'did the job touch the work' was answerable without instrumenting the job. A drainer whose backlog is only knowable from its own ledger cannot be checked this way.
